opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think it's useful to break it into stages, because people tend to collapse them together and then they either overhype or underhype what's happening.

The first stage, which we've been in for a while now, is the model writes some fraction of the code. A year or two ago that was autocomplete, a line here, a function there. Then it became "the model writes most of the lines of code," and I've said publicly that inside Anthropic, for a lot of teams, that's basically true now. But "the model writes 90% of the lines" is not the same as "the model does 90% of the job." Those are really different statements, and I think a lot of the confusion comes from conflating them.

Software engineering is writing code, but it's also figuring out what to build, understanding a large existing codebase, making architectural decisions, debugging something weird in production at 2am, coordinating with other people, reviewing, testing, deciding when something is done. Each of those is a separate capability, and each one is falling at a somewhat different rate. So you get this staircase. The model writes the code, then it can run the tests and iterate on its own. Then it can take a well-specified ticket and close it end to end. Then it can take a vaguer ticket and work out what was actually meant. And eventually it can operate over days or weeks on a project with something like the judgment of a senior engineer.

What I'd emphasize is that the thing that's been changing fastest, and I think is underappreciated, is task horizon: how long the model can work coherently on its own before it goes off the rails or needs a human to course-correct. That went from minutes to hours, and the trend line points toward days. Once you can work for days on your own, check your own work, and recover from your own mistakes, you're no longer a tool the engineer uses. You're much closer to being the engineer, with the human acting more like a manager or a tech lead.

Now, does that mean software engineers disappear overnight? I don't think so, and I want to be careful here. There's a comparative advantage dynamic. Even when the model does 95% of the work, the remaining 5% becomes the bottleneck, and humans get enormously leveraged on it. So for a while I'd expect productivity per engineer to go way up, maybe without employment dropping much. But I'd be lying if I said that lasts forever. When the model can do the last 5% too, it's a genuinely different world, and I think that could come faster than most people's intuitions suggest. Not certain, but plausibly within a small number of years.

And the reason I care about this so much, beyond the economics, is that software engineering is the closest thing to AI research itself. If models can do end-to-end software engineering, they can increasingly do a lot of the work of building the next model. That's the point where the feedback loop starts to tighten, and it's one of the main reasons I think we need to get the safety, interpretability, and policy pieces right now rather than later.

r001.rationale: It separates models writing code from progressively handling broader work, including tickets and long-running projects end to end.

r002.rationale: It describes remaining human work becoming a bottleneck and the human shifting toward a manager or tech-lead role, but does not clearly state that new tasks arise for engineers as automation advances.

r003.rationale: It predicts the model will eventually handle the “last 5%,” but does not identify that work as the new tasks that arise for engineers as automation advances.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the way to look at it is that there's a spectrum, and we've been moving along it faster than most people expected, including me.

A couple of years ago, the model was basically autocomplete. It would finish a line, maybe a function. Then it got to the point where you could describe a feature and it would write a reasonable chunk of it, but a human had to be in the loop constantly, checking, fixing, integrating. Now we're at the stage where the model can take a task, navigate a large codebase, make changes across many files, run the tests, see the failures, and iterate on its own for a meaningful amount of time. Inside Anthropic, a very large fraction of the code is now written by the model, and the engineers are increasingly acting more like reviewers and directors than typists.

The thing I'd emphasize is that "writing code" was never really the hard part of software engineering. The hard part is understanding what you're trying to build, holding the context of a large system in your head, figuring out why something broke, deciding what to prioritize, and coordinating with other people. So the progression to end-to-end automation isn't mainly about the model producing more lines faster. It's about the model being able to operate over longer horizons, with more context, and with more judgment. Each of those is improving, and they compound.

If I had to decompose it, there are a few dimensions. One is task length: how long can the model work autonomously before it drifts or gets stuck? That's been roughly doubling on some fairly regular cadence. Another is reliability. If a model succeeds ninety percent of the time on each step, a twenty-step task fails most of the time. Getting the per-step reliability very high is what unlocks long chains. A third is the ability to use tools and environments the way an engineer does: run things, read logs, look at the actual state of the world rather than guessing. And the fourth, which is the most subtle, is taste. Knowing when a design is bad, when a test is actually testing something, when to push back on the spec.

I do think we'll get to a point, and it's not very far away, where a model can do most of what a strong software engineer does over the course of a day or a week, with a human setting direction. That doesn't mean software engineers disappear. It means the leverage of each person goes up enormously, and the job shifts toward the parts that are about judgment and intent. But I'd be lying if I said that transition will be smooth for everyone, and I think we should be honest about that.

The other reason I care about this so much is that software engineering is the first domain where the models are automating the work of building the models themselves. That's the thing that could make the whole process go faster than people are planning for. So it's not just a question about one industry. It's a question about the rate of progress in AI as a whole.

r001.rationale: The response separates earlier code-writing assistance from the later stage of models handling broader engineering work, including navigating codebases, testing, and iterating autonomously.

r002.rationale: It says engineers’ jobs will shift toward judgment and intent, but does not clearly state that new tasks arise as automation advances.

r003.rationale: It predicts models will do most of a strong engineer’s work with a human setting direction, but does not say AI will eventually automate the new tasks described in r002.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a distinction between writing code and doing the whole job of a software engineer. Writing code is a very important part of that job, but you also have to understand what someone wants, figure out how the existing system works, decide what to change, and then check whether the change actually solved the problem.

You can imagine a model that’s very good at implementing a function when you give it a precise specification, but that still needs a person to decide which function to implement. The progression toward end-to-end engineering is about the model taking responsibility for more of that surrounding process.

A big part of this is how long it can work reliably. If it makes a mistake after five minutes and a human catches it, that can still be incredibly useful. If you want to hand it a project that takes several days, it needs to notice when it’s going down the wrong path, test its assumptions, and recover from mistakes. Being able to write each individual piece of code doesn’t automatically give you that.

So I’d expect a progression where humans delegate increasingly substantial tasks. First it’s a function, then it’s a feature, then it’s a project. And the interesting threshold is when supervising and correcting the system takes substantially less effort than doing the work yourself, even for tasks where you haven’t spelled out every step.

r001.rationale: It explicitly distinguishes writing code from taking responsibility for the broader software engineering process, describing them as different stages of progress.

r002.rationale: It describes parts of the existing engineering process beyond writing code, but does not state that new tasks arise for engineers as AI automation advances.

r003.rationale: It predicts AI will take on more of the surrounding process, but does not clearly predict automation of new tasks that arise for software engineers.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a distinction between writing code and doing software engineering. Writing code is one part of a much larger loop: figuring out what someone actually wants, understanding an existing codebase, making a change, testing it, and dealing with all the things that break downstream.

You can have a model that’s very good at the individual coding task but still needs a person to keep that loop on track. The harder question is: how long can it work independently before it makes a mistake that it can’t recover from? Can it notice that its approach is wrong, go back, and try something else? Can it resolve an ambiguous requirement instead of confidently implementing the wrong thing?

So I’d expect the progression to look like increasingly large units of delegation. First you’re asking for a function, then a feature, then you’re handing over an issue and expecting a tested change. Eventually you’re describing an outcome and letting the system manage much more of the process.

And there’s a second transition, which is organizational. Even when the model can do the work, you need ways to give it access, verify what it did, and decide which decisions require human judgment. So I wouldn’t identify end-to-end automation with a particular level of code-generation ability. It’s the reliability of the whole process that matters.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes individual code writing from the larger software engineering loop and describes progress toward delegating increasingly large units of work.

r002.rationale: It says people will need to provide access, verify work, and decide which choices require human judgment, but does not state that new tasks arise for software engineers as automation advances.

r003.rationale: It predicts that systems will manage more of the process, but does not clearly say AI will eventually automate the new tasks that arise for software engineers.
